expect.statement: Randomized evidence on antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, as identified by a systematic review and network meta-analysis with searches to June 2020, consists of six small, short (21 to 42 days), single-site trials with 395 participants in Thailand, Iran and China, mostly inpatients and mostly men, each comparing two of six antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); none had a placebo or no-medication arm, and two are titled as trials in amphetamine psychosis. Each trial reported no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms, and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well. Chaining the trials through their shared drugs, the network meta-analysis estimated that olanzapine (standardized mean difference −1.09, 95% CI −1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine (−0.86, −1.61 to −0.11) reduced symptoms more than risperidone and that aripiprazole did worse than four of the other drugs; these are indirect estimates only, rated low certainty by the authors because data came partly from open-label trials and the trials differ in participants and design, and both advantages over risperidone rest on one open-label trial of haloperidol against risperidone with 44 participants. Dropout did not differ, but its intervals were too wide to be informative. Because no trial had a placebo arm, these trials cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; the one placebo-controlled trial the review found, of aripiprazole in people whose psychotic symptoms had already subsided, was excluded. Side effects were not pooled; as narrative reviews describe it, the one trial included in a 2009 Cochrane review found fewer extrapyramidal side effects on olanzapine than on haloperidol. Two narrative reviews state that acute psychosis usually resolves with abstinence alone, citing early studies of amphetamine psychosis published between 1958 and 1980 or an online clinical reference entry. How often psychosis persists after stopping is described in section 9.

expect.grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence, now read through a systematic review and network meta-analysis (Srisurapanont et al., 2021; AMSTAR 2 low confidence on the first reading), so the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; the six trial reports themselves have not been read. Starts high. Risk of bias −1: two of the six trials were open-label (high risk in two domains) and allocation concealment was unclear in four; both indirect advantages over risperidone, and three of the four against aripiprazole, are chained through the open-label haloperidol–risperidone pilot trial (44 participants). Status replicated: six trials, from at least five independent groups (the two Chinese trials share authors), each reported no significant difference between its two drugs; the network's indirect differences come from one analysis and are not replicated. Later schizophrenia diagnoses ranged from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of more than 1,000 people after a first hospitalization, a figure three reviews give differently (38.8% at 5 years; nearly 40% within 6 years; and, if the systematic review's study of 1,116 people after a first hospitalization is the same cohort, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a study of 28 people); the systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, and a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. The pooled groups mix acute and persistent psychosis and current and past methamphetamine use; at least one comparison group with a primary psychotic disorder also used methamphetamine, two of the studies, from one research group, probably share participants, and the designs are cross-sectional. As reported in one narrative review of 12 direct comparisons (figures second-hand; at least three of its studies are also in the meta-analysis), more visual and tactile hallucinations in methamphetamine psychosis were found in one comparison of persistent psychosis (about 53 people per group), and a second comparison, of lifetime symptoms in 284 people who all had methamphetamine dependence, is reported in opposite directions in the review's table and text; in one comparison of acute psychosis (33 vs 69 people), voices conversing were more frequent in methamphetamine psychosis (48.5% vs 20.3%) and thought broadcasting in schizophrenia (42% vs 24%, significant only after adjusting for age). expect.statement: In observational studies, mostly cross-sectional and mostly in treatment, psychiatric, emergency or criminal-justice samples in which the comparison group often also used other drugs, people with an amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) had higher odds of psychosis than people without one: odds ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%) in studies that adjusted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk. The review grades this estimate at its lowest level of evidence (cross-sectional associations within samples of people who use drugs); its four studies were of young offenders, people in methamphetamine rehabilitation, people using methamphetamine at least monthly, and people released from prison (a cohort): in two of them everyone used methamphetamine, so the comparison was with methamphetamine use without a use disorder, and for the prison cohort the review reports no significant relation with later primary psychosis (later substance-induced psychosis was raised). Unadjusted estimates were 3.0 (1.9–4.8; 13 studies, I² 90%) for use disorder and 2.0 (1.3–3.3; 7 studies, I² 80%) for any use; the review's authors consider unadjusted estimates likely inflated by co-occurring risk factors, and comparisons made within samples of people who use other drugs likely to understate the difference from the general population. In post hoc subgroups the association was stronger for psychotic symptoms than for diagnosed psychotic disorders; for any use, the association with a diagnosed disorder was not statistically clear (1.3, 1.0–1.9). Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis. In a general-population birth cohort in Christchurch, New Zealand (962 to 1,025 people at each of five interviews from age 18 to 35), use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants in a period went with reporting at least one psychotic symptom in the same period: odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted and 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for childhood and family factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; the outcome was self-reported psychotic experiences on checklist and interview items (35–42% of the cohort reported at least one in each period to age 25), not diagnosed psychosis, and use and symptoms were reported for the same periods, so this cohort cannot show which came first either. The higher odds were concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (2.85, 1.21–6.69, adjusted for childhood and family factors only; about 1.3 and not statistically significant for less frequent use). expect.plain: Severe meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: agitation, wide pupils, a racing heart, high blood pressure and fast breathing. Less often there is very high body temperature, chest pain, seizures, muscle breakdown, or heart, liver or kidney failure, and some people die. This picture comes from two reviews of hospital emergency studies and case reports; we have not yet checked the original studies, and some of them concern amphetamine rather than meth. How often each sign appears differs a lot between studies and settings: a racing heart was found in 42 of 100 patients in one study and in 85 of 100 in another, and psychosis in 12 to 80 of 100. Neither review says how many patients die. One review notes that many meth-related deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide. Whether high body temperature predicts death has not been studied in the sources we have read.
expect.statement: In emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre series and in case reports, seen only through two reviews (figures second-hand; the primary studies have not been read), acute methamphetamine toxicity presents with sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose reported frequency varies several-fold between studies and settings. A narrative review describes the common features, from case reports, as agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure, with coma and seizures less frequent, and deaths in case reports are attributed most often to pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia. For non-fatal presentations it gives agitation in about 20%, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4%, from a few series, some of them of amphetamine, without denominators. A systematic review of 23 studies (searches 1990–2017; 17 from the USA, 7 of them from one centre) could not pool any clinical feature, because the studies measured them inconsistently; study by study it lists tachycardia in 42% and 85% and hypertension in 6.4% and 69% of presentations (two studies), acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain, psychosis in 12% (two studies) to 80% (60 people at a psychiatric emergency service), agitation in 13% to 48%, aggression in 18% to 50% and suicidal thoughts or behaviour in 6% to 50%, mostly without stated denominators. Neither review gives a case fatality among presentations or compares fatal with non-fatal cases, so whether higher body temperature predicts death among people who present is not established; the narrative review cites forensic studies suggesting that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide. set.plain: Meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: agitation, wide pupils, a racing heart, high blood pressure and fast breathing. Other signs include very high body temperature, chest pain, muscle breakdown, and heart, liver or kidney failure; seizures and coma are less common, and some people die. Whether high body temperature predicts death has not been studied in the sources we have read.

expect.plain: A large US survey from the early 1990s counted, for each kind of drug, how many of the people who had ever used it had ever been dependent on it. More than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths not involving opioids also rose, from 3,220 to 7,051. The death code (ICD-10 T43.6) covers psychostimulants other than cocaine; the authors report that about 85–90% of such certificates mention methamphetamine. These 2015–2019 figures (ages 18–64, DSM-IV) are not comparable with the 2024 survey figures shown in this section (ages 12 and over, DSM-5). Counting all ages, overdose deaths that a later analysis of the national death records labels methamphetamine-involved (its ICD-10 codes are given only in a supplement, not read) rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (crude rate 0.20 to 10.41 per 100,000; 2023 data provisional). The increase averaged 18.5% a year, was steepest in 2018–2021 (37.4% a year) and slowed to 3.4% a year (95% CI 0.2–6.8) in 2021–2023. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US survey figures use different methods and are not directly comparable. Newer death records for all ages show that deaths involving meth kept rising, from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, but the rise slowed after 2021. Deaths involving both meth and fentanyl rose fastest. These newer counts come from the same death records and include all ages, so they extend the earlier figures rather than confirm them.

expect.plain: Three trials have compared the antidepressant mirtazapine with a placebo in people with meth dependence. Two small trials by one San Francisco team, in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (and a few transgender women) who also had weekly counselling, found that mirtazapine may lower the chance of a meth-positive urine test by roughly a quarter to two-fifths. In the larger of those two trials, the share of people who stopped using did not clearly differ between the groups. A larger trial by a different team (one of its researchers also worked on the first San Francisco trial), at six clinics in Australia, also included women and people with symptoms of depression. People given mirtazapine reported using meth on about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people given placebo, but both groups still used on most days, and saliva drug tests showed no difference. In all three trials most people kept using and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine; in the Australian trial weight gain was too, and more people stopped taking it. Two other, short trials of mirtazapine for withdrawal symptoms are a separate question, described elsewhere in this section.
expect.statement: In three placebo-controlled trials in people with methamphetamine dependence or moderate to severe methamphetamine use disorder, mirtazapine was followed by somewhat less methamphetamine use than placebo on each trial's primary measure, although most participants kept using. Two trials from one San Francisco team, in men who have sex with men without current major depression (mean baseline CES-D depression scores about 17 and 20) with methamphetamine dependence who all received weekly counselling (60 men treated for 12 weeks; 120 cisgender men and transgender women treated for 24 weeks and followed 12 weeks after stopping), found a lower modelled weekly probability of a methamphetamine-positive urine: relative risk 0.57 (95% CI 0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks in the first trial and 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks in the second, with net relative risks of 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) 12 weeks after medication stopped. Most urine samples stayed positive in both arms (66% vs 78% of samples provided at week 12 of the second trial), end-of-treatment abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8%; OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61), adherence measured by electronic pill containers was below 50% in both arms, and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine. These two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so they are not independent replications of each other. A larger trial from a different team, one of whose authors is also an author of the first trial (344 adults randomized and 339 treated at six Australian public clinics; 37% women and 49% with a PHQ-9 depression score of 10 or more; given referral information and free to use other services, with no trial counselling described; treated for 12 weeks), found 2.2 fewer self-reported days of use in the past 28 days at week 12 than with placebo (95% CI 0.2–4.2; rate ratio 0.89, 0.80–0.98), from baseline means of 23.1 and 22.0 days, leaving both arms using on about 16 to 17 of 28 days (editors' calculation). It found no difference in methamphetamine-negative oral-fluid tests (13.2% vs 12.0% of samples; difference 1.3 points, −4.7 to 7.2) or in depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour or quality of life; drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine, 23% vs 15% stopped the medication for reasons related to it, and no outcome after the 12 weeks of treatment is reported. These trials treated methamphetamine dependence over months; the short trials of mirtazapine for the withdrawal period itself, reported in the claim on medicines for withdrawal, are different trials: pooled, they showed no difference from placebo in discontinuation, and one of them reported lower withdrawal scores, a result the review could not pool.

Risk of bias, one level: in the first trial the registered primary outcome was changed from feasibility to efficacy during recruitment; in the second, 34–41% of urine results were missing at each assessment, with more dropout on mirtazapine, and the analysis assumes data missing completely at random; in the third, the only significant result is on self-reported use, drowsiness (47% vs 33%) could have revealed allocation, no blinding check is reported and the article does not describe allocation concealment. This between-trial difference is a separate problem from the third trial's reliance on self-report, which is counted under risk of bias. Indirectness no longer rated down: the Australian trial adds women, people with depressive symptoms and public clinics without trial counselling, and the outcomes are measures of use; people taking antidepressants, pregnant people and people with a recent suicide attempt remain excluded. A later review of bupropion trials found about one-tenth fewer meth-positive urine tests than with placebo, but this is uncertain: it treated every test as if it came from a different person, part of the data came from a trial that also gave a second medicine (naltrexone), and for bupropion on its own the result could also mean no effect. Stimulant medicines such as dexamphetamine or methylphenidate were not part of this comparison; in the same review, four of six trials of methylphenidate reported fewer positive urine tests than a placebo, each measured in its own way, and two found no difference.
